claims.text: The base HfNbTaTiZr alloy is an equiatomic five-component alloy.
The target bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen as an impurity.
The target specimens contain inherent point defects.
The proposed framework will combine defect-inclusive ab initio data with physics-informed machine learning to parameterize electron-scattering rates.
The defect-inclusive calculations will explicitly represent oxygen-impurity scattering and temperature-dependent electron–phonon interactions.
Electrical transport from 0 to 200 K is dominated by impurity-driven quantum scattering.
From 300 to 1200 K, phonon scattering interacts with oxygen-related defect dynamics.
The spatial distribution and local environment of oxygen impurities modify electron-scattering rates and effective electronic conductivity.
At 0–200 K, oxygen impurities act as additional scattering centers and enhance electron scattering.
At 300–1200 K, oxygen-induced defect scattering combines with thermally activated phonon scattering to modulate electron transport.
The model will adjust scattering rates as functions of oxygen-defect concentration and temperature.
Predicted conductivity will remain within ±10% of experiment throughout both specified temperature regimes.
The model will capture a crossover from impurity-dominated scattering at cryogenic temperatures to combined phonon and defect scattering at elevated temperatures.
The physics-informed machine-learning model will outperform traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
Traditional analytical conductivity models assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Traditional perfect-crystal models typically overestimate conductivity because they neglect oxygen-impurity scattering.
The proposed accuracy claim is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model may not transfer directly to substantially different oxygen concentrations or other high-entropy-alloy systems.
Defect interactions and limitations of defect-inclusive datasets are sources of predictive uncertainty.
The hypothesis is falsified if conductivity error exceeds ±10% in either temperature regime or if improvement over the perfect-crystal baseline is not statistically significant.
